query: I am looking for a strategy to improve the mechanical performance of a multi-principal element alloy family that currently suffers from brittleness at room temperature. Specifically, I need a hypothesis for a processing route that can simultaneously enhance both yield strength and tensile ductility without the conventional trade-off, along with the expected structural evolution and a falsification experiment to distinguish this from standard thermal treatments.

generation.hypothesis: A multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) suffering from room-temperature brittleness can simultaneously achieve enhanced yield strength and tensile ductility by processing it into a two-hierarchical heterogeneous lamellar structure (HLS) via heavy cryo-rolling followed by non-isothermal annealing. This route exploits the back-stress strengthening mechanism arising from strain gradients between soft FCC and hard B2 (or L12) domains, which delays necking and suppresses brittle fracture without the conventional strength-ductility trade-off.
generation.material_initial_state: Brittle multi-principal element alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy) in as-cast condition with coarse lamellar microstructure, exhibiting low yield strength (<1 GPa) and limited ductility (<15%) due to coarse grain size and lack of strain gradient hardening.
generation.intervention: Multi-pass cryo-rolling (up to ~90% thickness reduction at liquid nitrogen temperature) followed by non-isothermal annealing (e.g., 660–740 °C for 1 h) to inherit and refine the lamellar structure into a two-hierarchical configuration: submicron grains within lamellae and micron-scale alternate lamellae.
generation.conditions: Room temperature tensile testing (strain rate ~10^-4 to 10^-3 s^-1); cryo-rolling at liquid nitrogen temperature; annealing in inert atmosphere; alloy system with FCC/B2 or FCC/L12 dual-phase character and moderate stacking fault energy.
generation.structural_mediator: Two-hierarchical heterogeneous lamellar structure with soft FCC domains and hard B2/L12 domains, generating significant strain gradients and geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) at domain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Back-stress strengthening from stored GNDs at soft-hard domain interfaces enhances yield strength, while strain gradient-induced work hardening delays necking and promotes uniform elongation. The hierarchical constraint effect prevents premature crack propagation by arresting microcracks at domain boundaries.
generation.predicted_outcome: Yield strength >1.4 GPa and tensile ductility >14% (elongation to failure), with a sustained strain-hardening rate over a wide plastic strain range, outperforming conventional thermally treated counterparts.
generation.baseline: Conventional annealing or cold-rolling without cryo-conditions results in homogeneous ultrafine-grained structures with high strength but low ductility (<10%) due to limited strain hardening capacity and absence of back-stress effects.
generation.boundary: Applicable to MPEAs with dual-phase (FCC/B2 or FCC/L12) microstructures and moderate stacking fault energy; ineffective for single-phase alloys or those with very high/low stacking fault energy where twinning or transformation mechanisms dominate.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal annealing temperature and rolling reduction may vary with alloy composition; excessive annealing may coarsen the hierarchical structure, reducing back-stress effects; cryo-rolling may introduce residual stresses that affect reproducibility.
generation.falsification_experiment: Process a batch of the MPEA using standard cold-rolling (room temperature) followed by isothermal annealing at the same temperatures as the cryo-rolling route. Compare the resulting microstructure (via TEM/EBSD) and mechanical properties (tensile test). If the standard route produces a homogeneous ultrafine-grained structure with lower ductility (<10%) and no significant back-stress hardening (measured via cyclic loading-unloading tests), while the cryo-rolling route yields a two-hierarchical structure with high back-stress and superior ductility, the hypothesis is supported. Conversely, if both routes produce similar properties, the cryo-rolling mechanism is not unique.
